utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may be seated. You do not have your headsets on but you can see my gesture, so I am sure you understand what I mean. We are meeting for a status conference. First, let me ask whether the accused hear me -- do you hear me -- in your own language? Please remain seated. Do the interpreters hear? Mr Kordic, do you hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KORDIC
utterances.text: Thank you for asking. We hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CERKEZ
utterances.text: I can also hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Defence? The Prosecution? You do not have to identify yourselves -- we know one another. The first comment I would like to make is that this is a status conference which had been scheduled. You know how the judges of this Trial Chamber are interested in ensuring that the proceedings go forward as quickly as we would like them to. However, you see that we are wearing our robes, we are not wearing civilian dress. We have many things to say during this status conference because certain things have occurred since the last time we met. Two things happened -- two submissions, one from the Office of the Prosecutor and one from the Defence. In respect of what came from the Office of the Prosecutor, this was a request for permission to amend the indictment. In a few moments, we will ask the Prosecutor not to tell us about the content of the amendment, because he could only do it according to the text and without the Defence being here, but at least give us the scope of the changes to the indictment and then there is the request for disqualification, which was presented by the accused and the defendants -- that is the disqualification of two judges of this Trial Chamber, Judge Riad and myself. The Tribunal, like all Tribunals, is familiar with the request for disqualification and the request will be responded to according to the procedures in place in this Tribunal, but since this is a public hearing I would like to say that the judges' concern has always been to ensure, once again, despite any difficulties that we have here -- physical difficulties -- that is we have only one courtroom for the time being -- to be sure these trials move forward quickly. Therefore I wanted to take advantage of the fact this is a public hearing to say if the Kordic hearing has not yet begun it is because we are first of all being asked for authorisation to amendment the indictment, which is not a request from the judges but from the Prosecution, and also a request for a disqualification of the judges, which does not come from the judges but from the Defence. All these motions are things you are entitled to ask for -- both the Prosecution or the Defence. You use your rights as you feel they should be used, but you should remember that, when one uses or makes use of a right, this also has to take into consideration the time periods for them and, therefore, this means that the trial will experience a certain amount of delay, which cannot be avoided. First of all, as regards the disqualification, it will not be decided on here -- will not be reviewed by the judges themselves but I wanted to say to the Defence that, by taking -- making use of its rights and doing what it considers best for the accused, if the judges who are speaking to you now -- I am speaking not only for myself but on behalf of my colleague Judge Riad, if we are to be disqualified or if we disqualify ourselves other judges will take over the case. So the public understands what is going on, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence has stated that there is a provision for the disqualification of judges; either judges who consider that they must disqualify themselves because they do not feel comfortable for many reasons -- we know this in our national legal system which means the judge would disqualify himself -- or there could be objective causes for his doing so. I need not say anything further about this, other than to be sure that the request is still up-to-date and I turn to the Defence and ask is there anything new in that request, but, for the time being, the request is in the hands of the Bureau of the International Tribunal, which is the only organ which has the authorisation for making that decision. Therefore, the Bureau will decide on the fate of that request. On that point, there are no specific comments to be added, I suppose, in your submissions, either the Defence or from the Prosecution. Is there anything new that you wanted to add? Go ahead, please. Please record your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr Naumovski, and I am counsel for the Defence, counsel for Dario Kordic. May it please your Honours, and colleagues, the Defence of Mr Dario Kordic abides by its motion for disqualification. We have provided all the arguments in our written motions but with respect to the Prosecution's response, I would like to make several additional comments, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, proceed, but be careful -- we are not talking about looking at the request for the disqualification of the two Judges Riad and Jorda at this point. If you have anything specific or formal to say, I have already told you that you do not have to make any comments about the disqualification of the judges. You filed a brief, I have told you -- I just want to be sure that it is up-to-date and I suppose it is, because it is 20 February, but I just wanted to be sure. Therefore, you do not have to make any comments and I would go even further and would say I would not like -- I think I am speaking for Judge Riad -- you can also respond in writing, and that would be submitted to the Bureau. You understand why I do not want to be involved in any discussion here about the excusing of the judges, but if we are talking about any factual changes or comments -- but it cannot go beyond that scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Absolutely. In fact, I was prompted by your question whether the Defence had any additional comments and in relation to the response which the Defence received last week, I was around but I did not get around to responding, but what I could do is I could, next week, provide a written reply to the response and then we can just proceed and conclude this today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then I would ask you to file your additional written comments very quickly -- not to the Trial Chamber but to the Registry, which will give it to the Bureau. I of course will not be part of the composition of the Bureau which will rule on the request. Therefore, if you agree, I invite you to supplement your comments, but as quickly as you can, perhaps tomorrow, if possible -- give it to the Registry, because I think that the Tribunal, or rather the Bureau of the Tribunal wants to settle the issue very quickly and I think that is in the interests of the accused, and in your interests as well as the Prosecution and the two judges who are here. This is my comment. Please do what you have to do quickly. Turning to the Office of the Prosecutor, do you have any factual or formal things that you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, President and counsel. No, we have nothing additional to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We now move to the second point in this status conference, which is the request for leave to amend the indictment. Mr Prosecutor, I give you the floor to explain what the substantive or form of changes you wish to make -- mostly form, I suppose. We give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President, my colleague Mr Scott will address the court in respect of that issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the court, my name it Kenneth Scott. It is my privilege to address this court for the first time. What I would like to do, your Honour, as the court has indicated, is to go through in a formal way how the amendments are different than the original indictment. I would take the opportunity briefly to say, and understanding the court's instructions, I believe we are on the same page, that it is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor as to the underlying facts and evidentiary material, that it would not be appropriate for Defence counsel to participate in the confirmation process, if you could view it in that respect. But we understand that, as to the motion for leave to amend, that any objections they may make such as that the amendment itself, for reasons unrelated to the underlying facts, are somehow unfair or prejudicial, we understand they could certainly make that sort of argument. If we were to get into -- I understand the court is not asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Scott. Would you like to explain how you interpreted the text that covered modification of the indictment -- I think it is Rule 50. You first have to ask for leave to amend the indictment -- is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is correct. We certainly -- we believe that is a process between the court and the Office of the Prosecutor, in a similar way as it would be for an original indictment. There has to be some sort of a process by which the court or some organ or component of the court confirms the charges, so to speak, in the amended indictment. But it is our position, your Honour, and we do not know of any law of any domestic jurisdiction that would be contrary, that, as to the charging decision made by the Prosecutor in proposing an indictment, and as to the confirmation process, whether there is sufficient supporting material for the indictment to be confirmed, it is our position that there is no Defence role and, with all respect, to be played in that process. Certainly once there is a charge -- at the moment, there is no charge, there is only the original indictment -- once there is a new amended indictment and there are charges that in fact have been filed and made of record with the court, and made a public document, we certainly understand that the accused have every right to contest the charges, to file whatever pre-trial motions they wish to make, but not to participate in the process in terms of the underlying -- and I am using the shorthand phrase, to say the "confirmation" process that would be similar to what takes place in an original indictment. I think we are together on that, in the sense that the court has asked for us to address essentially the form and scope of the indictment and the amendments and the changes and has indicated that it does not wish us to get into evidentiary detail in terms of the underlying supporting material -- at least that is what I understood the court to say. So, I guess with that proviso or further explanation, your Honour, and Mr President, I would go forward to indicate that it is clear that there have been some changes -- certainly no denying that -- there are some additional counts, and in some respects different counts in the proposed amendment indictment. I would tell the court, with all respect, that there has been in fact a substantial amount of additional evidence which has been gathered since 1995. Certainly the process is not static and there is -- there has also been substantial additional analysis of old evidence, if you will, and new evidence. We do believe, however, that with the one exception of the persecution count that has been added against Mr Cerkez in the second count of the amended indictment, that for all practical purposes the fundamental character of the indictments have not changed. The fundamental theory of the indictments are similar. We believe the defendants have always been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment, Mr Scott. I think that there is a prior point. You raise the question as to whether or not the Defence should be present during this explanation -- is that your prior point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At the same time you are saying to us that the Defence should not be here, but despite your concern you are explaining this indictment and you are going further and you have the Defence participating. Let me consult with my colleagues and see if we are interpreting the same way that you are in respect of this Rule. In that case the Defence would withdraw, of course once we have dealt with all the other matters in the status conference -- do you agree on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you would give me a moment, I would like to consult with my colleagues on the bench. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Unanimously the Trial Chamber interprets the Rules as you did, Mr Scott. Therefore, the explanations which you are going to give have to be understood as part of the explanations for the request for leave to amend the indictment and this should be done ex parte without the Defence being present. What I suggest, in agreement with my colleagues, is that we stop for one moment this point, but that we finish with the status conference in order to take advantage of the Defence presence and ask whether they have any other points they want to take up. First of all, let me turn to the Defence; are there any other points you would like to take up within the scope of the status conference and not in relation to the leave for a request to amend -- request for leave to amend the indictment. Please remind me of your names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVAVIC
utterances.text: Attorney from Rijeka. Mr President, I just wanted to add to this discussion, I really do not want to enter it, but we started with your last decision of 28 January 1998 by which we were invited to take part in the Prosecution's request to amend the indictment, so we responded to that and we expected to be given an opportunity to provide further arguments in response to this reply. So, without entering into the arguments about amending the indictment, I believe that we should be given an opportunity to give some comments in the sense of replying to the Prosecutor's request to amend the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You consider that, on the principle itself of authorisation, you have come -- let me turn to Mr Scott. You have heard the Defence comment, which is not requesting leave to discuss the contents of the amendment but to make some comments about the principle of authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I think it is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor that, as to the type of objections or opposition that would not be related to the underlying factual material or perhaps the legal theories, if you will, of the charging document, that such objections could be heard. I give an example as to -- while not agreeing with it, the example of, for instance, undue delay. An objection could be made on the grounds of undue delay which would have nothing to do with the underlying merits of the proposed indictment. There could be absolutely thorough factual support for the charge and apart from the merits of that charge the Defence could raise the argument that, because of unreasonable delay, the leave to amend should not be granted. So, I think it is a principle distinction that the Prosecutor certainly does not wish to take away any legitimate rights of the accused to object to parts of the indictment process that do not relate to confirmation of what I would call, if I can use the shorthand term, the confirmation process, just as they would not be able to participate in the confirmation of an original indictment with a single judge of the court. That is our position, your Honour -- if I have been clear, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On this point, with the Prosecutor's agreement, do you have some comments to make about this request for leave to amend the indictment but not the contents, which would go back to your request of 20 February 1998. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I was going to make a comment in that direction, and having heard the learned colleague the Prosecutor, I may not have understood him fully. There have already been some discussions that were held in this Trial Chamber about this leave to amend the indictment and I believe that the Defence can take part in it and as Defence counsel for Mr Dario Kordic I can say the following: during the first conversation with Mr Harmon, which we had during our first status conference, the Prosecution pointed out that it was going to amend the indictment. From this first announcement until today, about five months have elapsed. First the initial indictment, which was confirmed, was issued, that is, it was confirmed in November of 1995, and the accused Dario Kordic has been in detention since early August 1997. So the Prosecutor, about the time when Mr Kordic was detained, announced the amendment of the indictment. According to Rule 20, 21 the accused has the right to a trial without undue delay and he has the right to be informed of all the charges that were raised against him, so Dario Kordic was in detention for about five months before he was informed that the indictment was going to be amended. It only starts in October and continues today. We agree that it is up to the Prosecutor as to how they are going to structure their case. However, this cannot be at the expense of the right of the accused, because, by amending the indictment, the beginning of the trial is being delayed indefinitely. The Prosecution has advised the court that they are not prepared to discuss this issue and I do not want to be misunderstood. I think that it is a matter of tactics in order to slow down this proceeding and to put off the start of the trial itself. Without wanting to enter into the contents of the text, I understand the procedure here and the Defence also did not have enough time to familiarise itself with the supporting materials. Despite all of that, I say I have to point out that in the Prosecution motion for leave to amend the indictment, some well established facts were submitted and the original indictment charges a time period of 12 months, whereas now they are trying to extend it to 28 months. Also, it now expands the geographical area, which used just to be the Lasva River valley, to a much wider area. We submit that the Prosecutor -- since the time of the confirmation of the original indictment, more than two years and four months have passed, and, given the fact that the accused, Dario Kordic, has been in detention for over six months, we submit that the Prosecutor has passed the moment when they could amend the indictment. We also know that this amendment of the indictment has been hinted at a long time ago, but it took them five months actually to start the process, so we feel that this is a conscious delay of the proceedings. Certain Rules have been spelled out very clearly and among them are the rights of the accused, who has the right to be tried without undue delay. Of course, that is respecting the equal hands of both sides, the equal hands of both sides, and this has to be considered and, also, the Rules, or the principles of justice and fairness also need to be taken into account. Therefore, we believe that the Prosecution is too late in trying to amend the indictment, because only now are they trying to bring additional charges, which really would mean that it is a new indictment -- if the amendment of the indictment is such that it will really be a new indictment, I think that that may not be what the Trial Chamber has actually invited the Prosecution to do, which is to amend the existing indictment. This is in slightly greater detail than the Defence counsel of Dario Kordic has indicated in its written motion, but we felt it necessary to repeat that leave to amend the indictment should not be granted, because, by doing so, the accused, Dario Kordic, would be placed in an absolutely unequal position and his rights, envisaged by the Rules of Procedure, would be absolutely violated. May my learned friend forgive me, but I think that the first thought he expressed shows that he, by interpreting the Rules regarding any amendment of the indictment, is actually supporting inequality before the Tribunal and the Defence wishes to underline that equality is the fundamental principle which the Defence will abide by fully. We would also like to thank the Trial Chamber for allowing the Defence counsel to express its views regarding this motion for leave to amend the indictment, because it confirms the right of equality of parties, and due to which the Defence is given this opportunity to express its views regarding the motion for leave to amend. Without wishing to enter into any factual matters, which the Defence is familiar with, as it has received the draft amendment, I still feel it necessary to underline that, in this proposal, the geographical area is being expanded, as is the timeframe, and certain well known facts are referred to, which were familiar to the Prosecution at the time the original indictment was submitted. I will not of course go into those facts, because your Honours will have the occasion to review those when ruling on the motion of the Prosecution, but the Defence wishes to underline this, because that serves as the basis for the Defence's position, that this request is, first of all, absolutely too late and, secondly, that it changes the whole course of proceedings. Should the Trial Chamber rule in favour, then I am afraid that we will not be able to respect the timeframes that we agreed on at the first status conference. Therefore, the proposal of the Defence of Mr Dario Kordic is not to grant leave to amend the indictment, because, in our view, the Prosecution is too late in submitting this motion for leave to amend the indictment. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Kovavic, on behalf of Mr Cerkez you would like to speak -- not to repeat everything but of course it is proper for you to make formal comments. You will now be able to speak on behalf of your client, Mr Cerkez. Say whatever you wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVAVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President and your Honours. I, too, have no intention of going into the substance of the proposed amended indictment. I would, like my learned colleague, limit myself to certain conditions which we need to go into, or, rather, I would draw attention to a few points which I feel the Trial Chamber should bear in mind when making a ruling regarding the confirmation of the indictment. First of all, Defence counsel, or, rather, I as Defence counsel for the second accused, Mr Cerkez, appreciate very much the decision of the Trial Chamber of 28 January granting us this possibility to voice our opinion regarding the motion of the Prosecution seeking leave to amend the indictment. Nonetheless, unfortunately, the Rules do not envisage the Defence receiving the supporting material, which limits our possibilities regarding comments on the grounds or the supporting material for the indictment. However, from the Prosecution's motion itself dated 11 February, it is quite clear that some very significant and substantive changes are being proposed to the indictment. In a sense, one might say that this would in fact be a substitution of the original indictment by a new one. For us lawyers, numbers are not the best argument, but, in the original indictment six persons were charged for 13 counts on 13 pages of the brief. The proposed amended indictment charges two persons with 44 counts, each with 22 counts, on 22 pages of document. Therefore, this, in itself, shows that a much broader and larger document is involved. The Defence is not aware of whether such important changes are based on existing or new evidence, as we have not seen the supporting material. When talking about existing evidence, we are referring to the material the Prosecutor had in its possession at least during the initial appearance of the accused. The Defence believes that the proposed amendment is based on evidence which the Prosecutor had in its possession at the time the indictment was issued, so that, actually, the Prosecution is resorting to delaying tactics -- rather than being prompted by new evidence, which would require that he seek leave to amend the indictment. Accordingly, as Defence counsel, I would propose that the Trial Chamber rule on the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend only after the Prosecution manages to persuade the Trial Chamber that the proposed amendments are predominantly, in their majority, based on new evidence, because, if they are based on old evidence, then this is mere tactics, whereby the right of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial is being violated. Of course, the Defence counsel retains the right to prepare motions in the case that the Trial Chamber confirms the amended indictment, and with our motions we will contest the proposed amendments in their entirety or in parts. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Scott, this is the first part of our proceedings today having to do with the very principle of amending the indictment. You have heard the major argument presented by the accuseds' attorneys, namely, that this will all delay the trial. Let me remind you that on 27 January, when we had a status conference, you said that the trial could begin at the end of September. Are you still maintaining that date in respect of the changes that you request within the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is correct. The Office of the Prosecutor's position has not changed about that. We believe that, again, while indeed there have been some changes to the original indictment, that there should be nothing that would interfere with the trial going forward about that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. As for the second point, you heard what the Defence attorneys said in respect of this principle of granting leave to make the amendments. The attorneys are concerned, and are saying that, in the end, you are making significant changes to the scope of both the geographic and legal areas, which is not, in their opinion, a normal thing to do and that this might give you the authorisation to look for new evidence, whereas in fact everything should have been ready for the last year and a half or two years -- at least since 1995 when the indictment was confirmed. What do you think about what I have just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the court, let me just say that I do not believe the Office of the Prosecutor would be doing its job if we simply stopped investigating. The defendants, I would remind the court, were fugitives for a two-year period. During that time the Office of the Prosecutor has engaged in extensive investigation in the former Yugoslavia. I think it is absolutely the duty of the Prosecutor to continue to gather and act on new evidence and on new and fresh assessment of both old, if you will, and new evidence. I think that that sometimes can, if you will, cut both ways. I think the Office of the Prosecutor has shown an even hand, and, based upon reassessment of evidence, some accused have been released. I think it is absolutely consistent and in fact called for by the Articles of the Tribunal and the Prosecutor's professional obligations, that indeed investigation and analysis and assessment continue at all times, and the Prosecutor has acted consistent with those obligations. We submit, your Honour, that it is true and it is apparent on the face of the indictment that some of the geography has changed and some of the time periods have changed, but we return to the position that I stated to the court some minutes ago, that, in their basic character, the changes are not fundamentally different, that these accused have been on fair notice for a substantial period of time as to the nature and character of these basic charges and that the amended indictment, which we believe to be superior and we believe are appropriate, or certainly we would not have tendered, it is nonetheless consistent with the basic theories of Prosecution that were in the original indictment. If the court wishes, we can proceed on a count by count basis. I do not know if we need to do that at this particular point. I remind -- I would respond to several points by the Defence. There was early notice -- in fact there is a record of 21 October 1997, with Defence counsel, in which the Prosecutor's intent to seek an amendment was stated. This is not something that has come about lately; it was stated literally within days of the defendants, the accused, coming into custody. I submit to the court that, given the complexity of these investigations, the complexity of these facts, it is not unreasonable for the Prosecutor to have taken something less than three and a half months from the date of custody to filing its proposed amendments on 11 February, as this court ordered us to. I do not believe in any way that that time can be characterised as unreasonable. We believe that the amendment process is legitimate; the Rules clearly contemplate the Prosecutor's ability to seek an amendment. Again, we submit that the time that has passed between custody -- not today's date -- the amended indictment was filed on 11 February and the time between the defendants coming into custody, after being fugitives for more than two years, and allowing a three and a half month time for an amended indictment of a complex nature to be filed is not at all unreasonable. I can assure learned counsel that this is not a tactical ploy. We believe it a principled position by the Office of the Prosecutor, that this is the way the process should work in terms of the issues about the confirmation process and that the underlying material should not in fact be debated; that the Office of the Prosecutor is committed to that position as a matter of principle. Again, I would submit to the court that I do not know of any domestic jurisdiction which allows the accused to participate in the charging decision. Certainly, once a defendant or accused has been charged, they can file whatever motions attacking the charges that they wish to, but they do not sit in the Prosecutor's Office or in the Chambers of the court and make the decision whether a charge should be filed. We submit, your Honour, that the amended indictment is absolutely appropriate. It accurately reflects these accused's conduct. It is timely, and it would be I think truly -- if I can use the word -- a shame if the Prosecutor was not allowed to amend an indictment after a continuing investigation in the former Yugoslavia for more than two years to reflect those facts. We do not have a trial date at this time. I understand that there may be certain parts of the amended indictment that the Defence will want to further respond to and investigate, but, your Honour, we submit that there is ample time between now and the end of September for them to do that. With that, your Honour, unless the court has additional questions or wants to proceed on any sort of a count by count analysis, I will stop. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Naumovski, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President. My learned friend has now provided additional argument contesting what we said a moment ago. I would agree immediately with my learned friend regarding what he said, that this was a very serious and complex case, but my friend forgot to mention what is most important and that is that, for a long time now, an almost identical, in terms of the facts, trial is under way; that is, the trial of General Blaskic. This fact throws fresh light on what has been said by my learned friend. The Prosecution, in the opinion of the Defence of Dario Kordic, has had in its possession, for a year and more, a whole series of evidentiary material, which it will logically use in the indictment against Dario Kordic, as has been announced in this motion, and it is in that context that the timeframe is being extended. Earlier, it was May 1992 to May 1993 and now it is November 1991 to 1 March 1994. If there had been no Blaskic case, we could agree in principle. Unfortunately, what we say stands, that this proposal is not timely; it is too late. The proposal to amend is not linked to the presence of the accused. The indictment was confirmed already in November 1995. Therefore, if the Prosecution, after a certain amount of time, found new evidence, then she should have sought leave long ago, regardless of whether the accused were in custody or not. I must also refer to another point mentioned by the Prosecutor, and which was also raised at our first status conference. I do not know why the Prosecutor is trying to present the success of the Defence as their success. Mr Santic and Skopljak were not released thanks to the activities or efforts of the Prosecution but exclusively to the efforts of the accused and Defence counsels. It was their attorneys who managed to achieve their release. Of course that does not prevent the Prosecutor from continuing its investigations -- that is quite understandable -- but I appeal to this honourable Trial Chamber to review the supporting material in that context. We have reason to believe that these are predominantly old materials, which the Prosecutor was familiar with long before it sought leave to amend the indictment. I must say, as Defence counsel of Dario Kordic, that I also fail to understand a sentence uttered by my learned friend, and that is that this Trial Chamber has really no other possibility but to accept the Prosecutor's motion for leave. The Defence feels quite the opposite. We see no reason why the Trial Chamber could not reject this motion. There was a decision at the beginning of this month in the Kovacevic case that was rejected and it is the right of the Defence to voice its opinion in that context, too. For this reason, in particular, I feel that the additional arguments submitted by my learned friend are unfounded and I stand by the proposal of the Defence counsel of Mr Dario Kordic that the Trial Chamber should reject the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend, on the grounds that the Prosecution held in its own hands, to put it figuratively, the whole case against Dario Kordic long, long before he came here, even, and it is in that context that we allege that the motion for leave to amend the indictment is in any case too late -- not timely. I understand the efforts of the Prosecution to carry out fresh investigation, to seek new evidentiary material, and thereby to strengthen indictments against the accused, but, in the opinion of the Defence, it is impermissible to use old evidence, or, rather, the evidence that the Prosecution has had possession of for a long time whenever the Prosecution sees fit. In our view, that is impermissible, because the right of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial, and to be informed immediately of the charges against him, is flagrantly being violated and therefore I propose that the motion be dismissed. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Kovavic, additional comments? Do not reargue, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVAVIC
utterances.text: Mr President, I will not. Thank you. Just two sentences in response to what has been said by Mr Scott. It has been reiterated that the Prosecution, at least from 21 October, has been stating its intent to amend the indictment. We are aware of that announcement. It has entered the record. The only question now is that, now that we have received the draft of the new indictment, is it the result of fresh evidence, new evidence? Our colleague has said that there is some new evidence, but we must ask how much new evidence? Because, if we are talking about very significant amounts of new material -- a very significant expansion of the indictment, or if we are talking about just a drop of new evidence, 1 per cent, then this small amount cannot be an excuse for waiting for so long. If we are really dealing with new evidence, then obviously the Prosecutor is entitled to seek a new indictment. So, I repeat once again: I appeal to the Trial Chamber to ask the Prosecution to state clearly which part of the amendments is based on the evidentiary material it had in its possession at the time of the original indictment, and to what extent is it new evidentiary material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Scott, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could make three very short points in response. Number 1, I believe the record will show that the dismissals were on the voluntary motion of the Prosecutor and not based on any Defence motion or effort. I think the court's records will speak for themselves. Secondly, in terms of the expeditiousness of trial, we are not coming in here asking for a trial date to change -- in response to the President's question a few minutes ago, we stated our position that, in terms of the trial date, we believe it fair and appropriate that the trial date be about the time that has been discussed in the prior court hearing. So the Prosecutor does not come here and is making no motion at this time to delay the trial date whatsoever. The issues of an expeditious trial are governed by international standards. I refer very briefly, without belabouring this issue, to the Trial Chamber's decision -- the second decision in the Blaskic case on a motion for provisional release, in which this court reviewed a number of applicable authorities, including the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights and found the type of time periods that are being discussed here to be well within -- well within the permissible periods of pre-trial detention. There are cases -- we are not advocating the position here, but there are cases in which up to a five-year detention period has been held not unreasonable. We believe in this case that we are well within the time of reasonableness, that the amendments are appropriate. My final point, your Honour, is that I think much of our point -- much of the Prosecutor's point is made by a comment by learned counsel that, indeed, had these defendants appeared and surrendered at the same time as Mr Blaskic, they would have been in the same trial. This trial would be going on, even now, and they would have in fact received a quicker trial, because that trial would be well under way at this time. The issue of the delay of this trial is not the conduct of the Prosecution Office in seeking what it believes are legitimate indictments or legitimate amendments, excuse me, but the efforts to side track and keep this Chamber from moving forward -- and I would submit that it was the Defence and not the Prosecutor which has filed a number of motions, including the motion to disqualify. We ask that the court again grant us leave to make the amendments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we are going to stop the proceedings here. Everyone has had a chance to say what he had to say. I think we have really looked at this issue, all the more so because the judges would need to consult about the issue. But this discussion has to be broken into two parts. We will only deal with the first part, that is having to do with leave to amend the indictment or not, which will mean we will not hear the Prosecutor today, because, if two of these Trial Chamber judges are disqualified, I think it would be better for any new possible composition of judges to hear the substantive arguments that the Prosecutor would want to present, which would be the basis for his amending the indictment. However, insofar as we, for the time being, are seized of the issue, the three of us judges do consider that they are legitimately seized of the previous question, which is a valid one, which is substantive and also formal. This is the only one that the three judges here today will rule on. Either we will be disqualified or not and, if we are, the new panel of judges will hear the arguments, should the composition of this Trial Chamber have given leave to amend the indictment, but it would be the new Trial Chamber that would be fully competent to rule on the contents of the indictment. We are not accused here, of course, but we will now continue with the ex parte discussion with the Prosecutor, who would then give us all of the reasons that would justify the modifications that he is asking for. I will now close this chapter, turning to my colleagues, and ask them whether they have any additional things they would like to say. As regards organisation of the trial, I think it might not be suitable to say anything else right now, unless you do have something to add, as part of the status conference. I think we have mixed things up a little bit today, but I think that the plenary has established a pre-trial judge, and this pre-trial judge will have many powers, which will help us all move things forward quickly. Mr Naumovski, do you have anything else that you would like to say in addition to what has already been said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, listening to your deliberations, I got the impression that, if I understood correctly, in order to speed up the process of a decision on the motion about a disqualification of two judges of this Trial Chamber and after a short consultation with my colleague, I am going to withdraw my reply to the Prosecution in response to our initial motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not quite follow what you just said there. The first point I can answer, I can understand. I wanted to say something about the first point. Things must be transparent here; since we have been asked to disqualify ourselves we asked the Bureau to study the issue, but that decision has not yet been taken. Otherwise we would not have had this status conference, or I would have given you the results, had a decision been taken. I simply allow myself to say that if you had any additional things that you wanted to add, that it would be best to do them tomorrow, because I believe that the Bureau will take its decision without any further delay. Now, I must say I did not understand the second part of your comment, which seems to be connected with the first. Would you please repeat what the second part was?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely, based on what you just said, which I listened to carefully, I am withdrawing the reply to the Prosecution's response to our motion for disqualification of the judges, and I am doing it precisely in order to speed up the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That seems proper, that is the best way to work. If we remain here, you will have time to perfect your arguments. Before closing this issue I would like to ask the Prosecutor if there is anything he would like to say about the Kordic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we end the hearing, I would like to ask the accused, are your detention conditions satisfactory to you, insofar as one can be satisfied with detention conditions? Mr Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KORDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for asking. Your Honours, thank you for your kind questions. In this regard, as I said before, I am happy with the conditions there and I am hopeful that the trial will start soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CERKEZ
utterances.text: Thank you for asking. I am feeling well and there are no problems and I would only wish for the trial to start as fast -- as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We have completed the status conference. Therefore we will see one another again, or not see one another again. That is not our decision. The court stands adjourned. (3.55pm)
